paragraphs: He said: When the discourse on reliance on God (exalted be He) has come before us, I saw fit to follow that with the explication of the aspects of the purification of the works of obedience for God alone, on account of what is in this of the clarifying of inner beings and the cleansing of hearts from the admixture that corrupts them, and of the safeguarding from the kinds of self-adornment leading to ostentation, to affectation, and to the flattering of created beings — as Elihu said: "Let me, I pray, lift the face of no man, and let me not give honor to the human being; for I do not know how to give honor — in a little while my Maker would take me away" (Job 32:21–22).
It is fitting now that I make plain the matters of the purification of action for God in six concepts:

1. **The first**: what the purification of action for God is. 2. **The second**: by what it comes about. 3. **The third**: in which kinds of action the purification for God is binding. 4. **The fourth**: how many genera of its corrupters there are. 5. **The fifth**: how their negation from the soul is to be carried out, that the purification for God may be made valid in the human at every act he undertakes for His face. 6. **The sixth**: on watchfulness over the imagination, and the guarding-against and reining-in of it.

As for the purification of action for God (exalted be He) — it is the aim, in the outer and the inner, in the work of obedience to God, at His face (exalted be He), seeking His satisfaction alone, to the exclusion of the satisfaction of created beings.

As for that by which the purification of action for God alone comes about: ten concepts. When they are made valid in the soul of the human, and verified, and made foundations for his obedience and roots for his action, then his purification for God (exalted be He) in them is completed; he turns to no other than Him, hopes in none but Him, and aims by them at none but His satisfaction.
**The first** — purification of the affirmation of God's unity (exalted be He), as has gone before in the opening of this book of mine.
**The second** — reflection on God's blessings upon him and their succession to him, as we have explicated there also.
**The third** — binding-oneself to obedience to God, as I have mentioned there also.
**The fourth** — singling Him out by reliance to the exclusion of created beings.
**The fifth** — the soundness of his certainty that benefit and harm are not in the discretion of any created being nor in his power, apart from the permission of the Creator (exalted be He).
**The sixth** — that praise and blame from people toward him be equal in his eyes.
**The seventh** — the abandoning of self-adornment for people.
**The eighth** — emptying his mind and his heart of the preoccupations of this world at the time of his work for the next world.
**The ninth** — watchful awareness of God (mighty and exalted) and shame before Him.
**The tenth** — taking counsel of the intellect in everything that caprice whispers in his heart, and acting on its judgment to the exclusion of the judgment of caprice.

As for the works that are completed by the purification for God when one undertakes them — they are the works of obedience aimed at the satisfaction of God (exalted be He): namely, the totality of the manifest obligations upon the limbs, in which the doer's directing of them to other than God is possible, so that his aim becomes self-adornment for people by them, the seeking of their honor for him, and their praise of him for performing them.

As for the duties of the heart — neither ostentation nor love of honor and praise is possible in them for whoever has bound himself to anything of them, since people have no knowledge of that from him; the one who undertakes them aims by them at the face of the One who is informed of them, namely God (exalted be He) only, as He said: "I, the Lord, am one who tries the heart, who searches the kidneys" (Jeremiah 17:10); and He said: "The hidden things belong to the Lord our God, but the revealed things belong to us and to our children" (Deuteronomy 29:28).

As for the genera of the corrupters of the purification of action for God (exalted be He) — they are three. **The first**: ignorance of God and of His blessing. **The second**: ignorance of the command of God and of His Law. **The third**: the whisperings of caprice and its signaling to the human of what makes this world beloved to him and removes him from the path of the next world.

As for the aspect of the corruption that ignorance of God brings to the works of obedience — it is this: that whoever is ignorant of his Lord does not worship Him with his heart. Only the one who is not ignorant of His command — and from whom benefit and harm are valid — worships Him. So if the one who is ignorant of God works some work of obedience, his aim in it is only the aim of the one who fears and hopes in people; he is worshiping people, not the Creator of people, on account of his ignorance of Him and the weakness of his discrimination concerning Him.

So too the discourse on the one who worships idols: it is his ignorance of God (mighty and exalted) that carries him to that. The idolater may even be more excellent than the showy actor in four respects.

**The first** — the idolater in this present age is not prohibited from the worship of idols by the hand of a prophet who would verify for him the corruption of his school by the signs and the demonstrations. The showy actor in the religion of God, by contrast, is refuted by what has been transmitted to him of the matters of the worship of God, and the prohibition of associationism with Him, and of reliance upon any other than Him.
**The second** — the idolater worships one who does not disobey God; the showy actor in the religion of God worships one who does not disobey God *and* one who disobeys Him among people.
**The third** — the idolater worships only one thing; the showy actor's objects-of-worship have no end.

**The fourth** — the idolater is not hidden from people in his affair, so they are warned of his harm by the renown of his disbelief in God; the showy actor, by contrast, is not manifest in his disbelief in God, so people are at ease toward him, and he is enabled to inflict upon them harms that another could not. He is the most malignant disease in the world. He is the one named in our language *ḥanef* and *yahir* and *mefuteh*.

As for the one who is ignorant of the command of God and of His Law — his action in obedience to God is not made pure for Him. For if he is ignorant of the aspects of obedience in the roots of the laws, how much more is he ignorant of the aspects of its completion by the purification of his heart in them for God (exalted be He). Whatever he undertakes of the work of obedience, his aim in it is other than God; he is like one who doubts the validity of its obligation upon him, since he has no knowledge of what binds his purification in it for God — as the early ones (peace be upon them) said: "An ignorant man cannot be sin-fearing, nor [an *am ha-aretz*] pious."

As for the whisperings of caprice and its signaling to the human in what corrupts the purification of his heart at his working for God — even when he is knowledgeable of God and of His Law — they are divided into two divisions. **The one of them**: thoughts by which it casts doubt upon his realities and confounds his certainty, so that no work is made pure for God for him. **The second division**: its disputing with him, by argument and proof, that whatever he undertakes and exerts himself in of work for God is not obligatory and not [in the way of certainty] for him; rather it directs him to work for this world and its people.

I see fit to explicate to you, of this, examples that point to the rest I have not mentioned of them, that people may be on guard against them and may purify their devotion to God (exalted be He) — as he said: "Let the wise hear and gain learning" (Proverbs 1:5).

That is, by my saying: it is fitting for you, O human being, to know that the bitterest enemy you have in this world is your caprice — mingled with the powers of your soul, mixed in with the temperament of your spirit, sharing with you in the management of your bodily senses, the one with access to the secrets of your soul and to what you keep in your inner being, the one whose counsel is sought in all your manifest and inward movements that arise from your choice, the one who watches the times of your heedlessness. You sleep concerning him, and he is not asleep concerning you; you are inattentive to him, and he is not inattentive to you. He has put on for you the garments of love and adorned himself in the dress of affection toward you, and he has come to be among the totality of your counselors, your guides, and your sincere friends. With the subtlety of his deception toward you, he runs toward what agrees with you in the surface of his hints and his signals — while he shoots you with the deadliest of his arrows.
His state with people is as Scripture said: "As a madman who shoots firebrands, arrows, and death — so is the man who deceives his neighbor, and says: Was I not joking?" (Proverbs 26:18–19).

Among the strongest of his weapons by which he fights you in the inward of your affair: that he aims to throw your realities into doubt, to admix what has been clear to you of certainty, and to disturb your soul with false imaginings and empty claims by which he preoccupies you from your welfares and overlays for you what was crystalline to you in your faith and your firm conviction. If you are on your guard against him, and have prepared against him the weapons of your intellect by which you fight him and ward off his arrows from you, you are saved and delivered from him by the permission of God (mighty and exalted). But if you have given the matter over to him and made your reins to his judgment, nothing of you will satisfy him short of your destruction in the two abodes and your eradication from the two stations — like what the Friend said about a branch from his branches and a person from his army: "For many are the slain she has cast down, and mighty are all her killed; the ways of Sheol are her house, going down to the chambers of death" (Proverbs 7:26–27).

Let no struggle against another distract you from struggling against him; no fighting against any other than him from fighting against him; no warring against the one who is far from you from warring against the one who does not depart from you; no warding off of the one who can reach you only by leave from warding off the one who needs no leave to come upon you.

It has been said of one of the righteous that he met a company of people returning from war against an enemy with the spoils, after a hard struggle. He said to them: "You have returned, by the praise of God, from the lesser struggle with the spoils. Now prepare yourselves for the greater struggle." They said to him: "And what is the greater struggle?" He said to them: "The struggle against caprice and its troops."

It is among the wonders, O my brother, that any enemy you have, when you have overcome him once or twice, has had enough of you and is preoccupied no longer with making war upon you, knowing the surplus of your strength over his strength; he is in a state of despair of overcoming you and gaining the upper hand. But caprice is not satisfied with overcoming you once or a hundred times — whether he overcomes you or you overcome him. For if he overcomes you, he kills you; if you overcome him once, he watches you the rest of your days that he may overcome you, as the early ones said: "Do not trust in yourself until the day of your death" (m. Avot 2:4). He does not consider it a small thing to overcome you in any fine point among the fine points of your affairs, that this may be a step-by-luring toward overcoming you in what is above it.

In proportion to that, it is fitting that you be in a state of guard against him: do not allow him anything of his demands of you; rather let the slight thing of your overcoming him, when you have overcome him, be great in your eye, and the trifle of his being defeated be much in your sight, that you may be lured by that toward what is above it. He is quick to be subdued to you and slight in firmness when you stand firm in opposing him, as Scripture said: "And toward you shall be his desire, and you shall rule over him" (Genesis 4:7). Let his affair not terrify you even if his followers are great; let his cause not awe you even if his helpers are many. For the root of his aim is the verifying of falsehood, and the meaning of his purpose is the establishing of the impossible. How quick his fall is, how near his destruction, if you are sharp to his weakness!
This is what the Wise One described, in his saying:

> A small city, and the people in it few; and there came against it a great king, who surrounded it and built against it great siege-works.  And there was found in it a poor wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city. (Ecclesiastes 9:14–15)

He described the human being as "a small city," because he is the small world. He described the instruments of his body and the traits of his soul as "people," and called them *few* on account of the magnitude of the human being's ambition and the length of his hope in this world, and the falling-short of his strength and the slightness of his perception of it. He described caprice as a "great king" on account of the multitude of his troops, his followers, and his retinues — for he encompasses all the matters of the human being in his outer and his inner. And his saying "and built against it great siege-works" — meaning the multitude of his evil thoughts, his vile imaginings, and his blameworthy assaults by which he aims at the destruction of the human being, as we shall go on to explicate in what we resume of this gate. And his saying "and there was found in it a poor wise man" — meaning the intellect. He described it as "poor" on account of the slightness of its followers and helpers, as he said of it: "And no man remembered that poor man" (Ecclesiastes 9:15), and he said: "And the wisdom of the poor man is despised" (Ecclesiastes 9:16). And along with its weakness, he described the swiftness of caprice's submission to it at its struggle, and the warding-off of its harm from the human being with ease — for a little of truth overcomes much of falsehood, just as a little of light dispels much of darkness. In this is an awakening to struggle against the appetites and to the standing-against caprice with diligence and zeal — for its weakness against the standing-against of the intellect has been made plain to us, and the swiftness of its rout before it — like the saying of Scripture: "The wicked bow down before the good, and the wicked at the gates of the righteous" (Proverbs 14:19).

The first thing in which caprice tries to throw doubt upon you, and to make manifest to you, is that your soul has no continuation apart from the body, and that it is corrupted by the corruption of your body, and that it has no existence after death — by ambiguities that do not stand at examination. Its purpose is that this may be a cause for you to seek the perishing pleasures and the passing appetites; you say what Scripture said of the people of this opinion: "Eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" (Isaiah 22:13). If you take counsel of your intellect concerning this school, the intellect will negate this opinion from you by the clear evidences mentioned by the early ones and by the traces of the prophets (peace be upon them).

When he despairs of throwing your soul into doubt, he aims to throw the Creator (mighty and exalted) into doubt for you, saying: "This world is not originated, not brought into being from nothing; it has not ceased to be in the state in which it is, and shall not cease to be so. Nothing in it is more rightly Creator than created, since the all is eternal-without-beginning; no obedience to another is binding by anything in it, since the all is *qadīm* and *azalī*." When the like of this comes upon you, return to your intellect; it will show you the corruption of this school from the discourse on the purification of unity-affirming for God in this book, by what makes you find that the world has a Creator who created it not from a thing. It is fitting for you to know that all that the Law has taken upon us concerning the matter of the Sabbath — the repetition concerning its keeping and remembrance, the promises and the threats — the purpose and aim in it is the negating of the school of the *Dahriyya* from our imaginings and the establishing of the concept of *ḥadath* (origination) and *ibdāʿ* (creation-from-nothing) and its firm conviction in our souls, since this is the sound opinion. Understand.

When he despairs of confusing this matter for you, he casts you into the kinds of associationism — like the school of the dualists, the school of the Christians on the Trinity, the school of the naturalists, and the school of the ignorant astrologers, in their varying schools. When it has been verified for you that the Creator (exalted be He) is one and eternal-without-beginning, as we have laid down in the opening of this book, all these doubts depart from you.

When he despairs of you in this aspect, he aims to deceive you concerning the obligation of obedience to God, and says to you: "Obedience is rendered by the obedient to the obeyed only at his need of him; the Creator (exalted be He) is not in need of His created beings nor needful of His made things; your obedience to God has no meaning and no purpose for the wearying-of-yourself in it." If you raise your sight by your intellect to what has come before us in the Gate of Reflection on God's blessings upon us, and in the Gate of the Obligation of Binding-Oneself to Obedience to God on account of them, this doubt departs from you, and you make obedience to your Lord obligatory upon yourself.

When caprice despairs of deceiving you by this aspect, he aims to throw you into doubt concerning prophecy, the Messenger, the canon of the Law, the aspects of its soundness and its bindingness. If you stand against him with your intellect, and fight him with the proofs that have come before in this book in the Third Gate of it, all those doubts depart from your breast; the meaning of revelation is verified for you, and the necessity of the Law and the sending of the Messenger with it, and the aspects of awakening to it.

When he despairs in this concept of throwing you into doubt, he throws you into doubt concerning the transmission. He says to you: "The rational and the written are both sound; but as for what the early ones have transmitted to you, it is only supererogatory — not binding to take it on." If you reflect with your intellect, you see that the rational and the written are both in need of transmission, in a strong and emphatic need; for neither of them is complete without transmission. The rational, if transmission has not bounded for us its quantity, its quality, its time, its place, and the rest of its accidents — that is not made valid for us from our intellects alone. So too the written: if transmission did not explicate for us the aspect of its reading, the interpretation of its language, the interpretation of its meanings, and their derivation, this would not be completed for us from the Book alone — as our early ones (peace be upon them) said: "By thirteen *middot* the Torah is interpreted"; and they said: "Tradition is a fence around the Torah" (m. Avot 3:13). And the Book itself has referred us, in all its branches, to transmission, in His saying: "If a matter is too wondrous for you for judgment…" (Deuteronomy 17:8); then He said: "And you shall inquire, and they shall declare to you the matter of the judgment" (Deuteronomy 17:9); and He said: "And the man who acts presumptuously, not listening to the priest who stands to serve there…" (Deuteronomy 17:12). When you stand upon this, the doubt departs from you, and the rational, the written, and the transmitted knowledge are validly established for you.

When he despairs of deceiving you from this aspect, he aims at it from the side of reward and punishment. He throws you into doubt first about reward and punishment in this world, saying: "Were reward and punishment running in this world along the path of justice, the unbeliever would not be blessed and the people of righteousness would not be tested in this world" — according to what was said by the one we mentioned in the Fourth Gate of this book. When the intellect uncovers for you the aspects of justice in the two matters which we have mentioned in the Gate of Reliance on God, this doubt departs from you, and your heart is calmed from his confusion.

When caprice despairs of overcoming us by this aspect, he throws us into doubt concerning the reward of the next world and its punishment, and aims at admixture and confusion for us by the slightness of its being explicated in our Book and the slightness of the appearing of its traces in it. When we reflect on what is in the books of the rest of the prophets concerning this — like "And the spirit shall return to God who gave it" (Ecclesiastes 12:7); and "And I shall give you ones who walk among these standing here" (Zechariah 3:7); and "How abundant is Your goodness which You have stored up for those who fear You" (Psalms 31:20); and "Eye has not seen, O God, beside You, what He shall do for the one who waits for Him" (Isaiah 64:3); and "And your righteousness shall walk before you" (Isaiah 58:8); and many like these — together with what is indicated by the traces of the early ones, and what may be perceived of it by the path of the intellect: our souls are calmed, and we lean upon the validity of the obligation of reward and punishment in the next world.

When caprice despairs of throwing us into doubt in all that has come before of mention, he aims to make us lazy concerning the works of obedience, and to preoccupy us with the matters of our this-world — of food, drink, clothing, mount, and the taking of pleasure in the kinds of bodily delights. If we obey him in the subsistence of which we cannot do without, he adorns to us the surpluses that follow upon subsistence — and makes beloved to us the luxury and the indulgence and the rivalry of kings and sultans and the people of their service in the resembling of them, the running upon their patterns, and the taking of their ways in the seeking of pleasures. When caprice sees from us eagerness for these and zeal toward them, he says to us the saying of the poet:
> When souls are great, > bodies grow weary in their pursuit.

And he says: "Roll up your sleeves, O deceived one; exert yourself, O bewitched one; serve this world and worship its people, that perhaps you may attain something of your purpose in it. Do not expose yourself to anything of the works of the next world except what may be a help to you in this world — by which the people of your time and their service among kings and the marketplace are pleased with you. Do not preoccupy your mind with the sciences except with what you may adorn yourself by before the people of your time, and dissemble by toward the great of those of your day among vizier, head of police, governor, and possessor of office: like the science of rare lexicography, the canon of prosody, the roots of grammar and poetry, the elegant traditions, the rare proverbs, the unusual hadith, and the use of the assemblies of the people of eloquence; the learning of speech with every rank among the ranks of people; the learning of astrology and judgment by it for the elect and the populace."

You take counsel of your intellect and seek its judgment; it informs you that if you turn aside from what concerns you of the science of the Law and the upholding of it — to the exclusion of the rest of the sciences — you perish; and nothing of what you have preoccupied yourself with profits you with God (exalted be He), apart from this. The Messenger (peace be upon him) has emphasized this upon you, in his saying: "And you shall not walk in the statutes of the nation" (Leviticus 20:23) — those whose practice is to look to the rulings of the stars and to omens and to divinations and to sorceries and the like, in which they take counsel — as Scripture said of them: "For these nations whom you are dispossessing listen to soothsayers and to diviners; but as for you, the Lord your God has not so allowed you" (Deuteronomy 18:14). The Messenger (peace be upon him) said: "Let there not be found among you one who passes his son or his daughter through fire, a diviner of divinations" (Deuteronomy 18:10) — pairing the one who passes his son and daughter through fire with the diviner, since this is hated by God (exalted be He) the like of that, and the two are weighed against each other in His abomination. The prophets repeatedly censured this in many places, with no need for us to establish here on account of its renown; Scripture said: "For there is no augury in Jacob and no divination in Israel" (Numbers 23:23); and the Friend said: "Not like these is the Portion of Jacob, for He is the Former of all" (Jeremiah 10:16) — together with what is in this of turning away from reliance on God (exalted be He), surrender to Him, and contentment with His judgment and His decree. For if decree and predetermination by lucks and ill-omens are referred to the rulings of stars and to omens and the like, that is associationism with God in its pure form, without fail; it leads to disbelief in God and to denying Him entirely.

If a speaker should say: "We have found Gideon son of Joash judging by augury, by the contention of the speaker and his supposition, in his saying: 'And Gideon came, and behold, a man was telling a dream to his fellow… and when Gideon heard the recounting of the dream and its interpretation…'" (Judges 7:13–15) — we say to him: God commanded him to do this since He knew of him the slightness of his confidence in his excellences and his self-deprecation; God deemed it well of him. Since this is so, this has gone forth from being augury. If he should say: "We have found Jonathan son of Saul, who patterned himself upon augury by the supposition of the speaker, in his saying: 'And Jonathan said to the lad bearing his weapons, Behold, we are crossing over to those men… if they say to us, "Wait until we come to you," then we shall stand still… and if they say to us, "Come up upon us…"'" (1 Samuel 14:8–10) — we say to him: it has come before in the discourse, before this, that Jonathan called upon God to make manifest his victory for Israel by his hand, in his saying: "And Jonathan said to the youth bearing his weapons: 'Come, let us cross over to the garrison of these uncircumcised; perhaps the Lord will act for us, for there is no constraint for the Lord to save by many or by few'" (1 Samuel 14:6). His saying "perhaps the Lord will act for us" is evidence that he beseeched, longed for, and called upon God (exalted be He) to grant him victory and aid him over the enemies. When God (exalted be He) knew the goodness of his intent — that what he aimed at to do was a welfare and a help for Israel — God answered him in what he sought from Him; gave him victory over his enemies; and made him a cause for the completion of victory and triumph over the rest of the Philistines. So this too has gone forth from being augury, by his calling upon God to give him victory and to give the nation victory, as in his saying "for there is no constraint for the Lord to save…"

If he should say: "We have seen the early ones censuring those who refrain from the study of astrology, in their saying: 'Whoever knows how to calculate the seasons and constellations and does not calculate, of him Scripture says: And there shall be lyre and lute, drum and pipe, and wine at their banquets — but the work of the Lord they regard not, and the deed of His hands they do not see' (b. Shabbat 75a, on Isaiah 5:12); and they said: 'From where do we derive that a person is bound to calculate seasons and constellations? As it is said: And you shall keep and do, for it is your wisdom in the eyes of the peoples (Deuteronomy 4:6) — what is the wisdom that is to the eyes of the peoples? Say: this is the calculation of seasons and constellations'" — we say to him: the early ones bound this from the saying of the Prophet, "Lift up your eyes on high and see who created these…" (Isaiah 40:26); and the Friend said, "When I see Your heavens, the work of Your fingers…" (Psalms 8:4). This is by way of reflection upon existing things, that we may infer from them that they have a Creator, powerful and wise, who created them not from a thing, and ordered them and made them firm by the most beautiful order and the firmest fixity. The obligation of reflection on them in this aspect — not to judge by them, nor to rule from them on lucks and ill-omens. Understand.

In the like of this and its likes, caprice aims to enter you in to corrupt you and overturn you. He says to you: "Beware sluggishness and silence, lest you be ascribed dullness and ignorance; let go of all the sciences, the multitude of their toil and the slightness of their benefit." If we do not open the door to the appetites at the start of the affair, and do not flatter him in the use of surpluses, and do not pursue them eagerly — and we respond to him that surpluses do not call us to any need of them, and there is in attending to the matters of our subsistence enough to occupy our souls; that if God enables us with surpluses without preoccupation of mind in them and the use of our thoughts upon them, we direct them to what is binding and to what is incumbent; and if not, we are content with subsistence and have no need of more — caprice is broken and routed.

If we obey him in this, he draws us up from rank to the next, until he overlooks us at perishing in this world and the next. This is like the first kind by which caprice throws into doubt the human who is weak in knowledge and acquaintance with God and with His Law.

As for when the human is knowledgeable of God and of His religion — caprice aims to introduce corruption into him and to admix his knowledge and his action by the path of argument and proof, from whatever he can of the rational, the written, and the transmitted; he proves to you what he directs you to by deceptive proofs whose premises are not truthful and whose conclusions are not necessary. If your intellect is clear, your knowledge strengthened in the path of demonstration and the aspects of guarding-against in disputation and debate, you make manifest the necessity of the error of caprice in his evidence and his proof; the truth is made valid for you, certainty is crystallized for you, your knowledge is purified of doubt, and your work of admixture. If you fall short of this, his deception is stronger upon you, his triumph more manifest, his rule over you more severe, his dominion over your outer and inner more emphatic — for he comes to you from the side of knowledge and runs you down the path of demonstration to which your intellect is at home; when he deceives your intellect, he leans upon it and uses it as a help against you in your reposing upon it in what its affair has been admixed for you, and your reliance upon it in what you have been ignorant of its meaning. When he gains hold of you and rules over you with the help of the intellect to him and its aiding-of-him in what he makes it imagine and depict to it of falsehood in the form of demonstration, he moves you from that rank that was nearest to the truth and in which the aspect of falsehood was hidden — to the next, in which the truth is less and the falsehood more; and so he never ceases to move you from rank to next, until he brings you to a rank in which the aspect of truth has been hidden and which is pure falsehood. Then he uproots you in this world, drops you from the ranks of the reward of the next world, and your knowledge becomes a burden upon you, your intellect a cause of your destruction — like what Scripture said: "Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and discerning before themselves" (Isaiah 5:21); and: "Behold, they have rejected the word of the Lord; what wisdom is in them?" (Jeremiah 8:9); and: "For the ways of the Lord are upright" (Hosea 14:10).

It has been said: "When the wise man walks the path of wisdom along its proper road, it becomes a medicine for every disease; when he turns aside with it from its proper path, it becomes a general disease for which there is no medicine and no healing." For this reason, the Law has been likened to fire — as Scripture said, "Is not My word like fire?" (Jeremiah 23:29) — for it illuminates the eyes by its brightness, as He said, "The commandment of the Lord is pure, enlightening the eyes" (Psalms 19:9), and "Your word is a lamp to my feet" (Psalms 119:105); and it burns with its heat the one who turns aside from its path after his knowing of it, as He said, "For with fire the Lord shall enter into judgment" (Isaiah 66:16); and "He shall rain upon the wicked snares" (Psalms 11:6); and "Then I said, I shall not remember Him, nor shall I speak again in His name; and it became in my heart like a burning fire" (Jeremiah 20:9).

So beware lest your foot slip from the path of the predecessors and the way of the early ones to innovation, the use of your own intellect, the singling-yourself-out by your own opinion, and your specialness in your analogical reasoning. Do not impugn your forbears in what they have transmitted to you of the aspects of your guidance, nor undermine their judgment in what they have laid down for you. There is no opinion that has dawned on you that they have not preceded you in knowing, and have not paused at every consequence-of-rectitude-and-corruption that it leads to. It may be that there has occurred first to your imagination an aspect of correctness in the school at the start of its affair, while the aspect of corruption that will come from it in its end has been hidden from you; you, with the slightness of your firmness, see its rectitude and do not see its error and the aspect of its corruption. The Friend said: "Do not move the boundary of old that your fathers set" (Proverbs 22:28); and he said: "Hear, my son, the discipline of your father" (Proverbs 1:8). And he said of the one who altered the customs of his fathers: "There is a generation that curses its father and does not bless its mother; a generation pure in its own eyes and not washed of its filth" (Proverbs 30:11–12); and he said: "The eye that mocks at a father and despises the obedience due a mother — the ravens of the valley shall pick it out and the young eagles shall eat it" (Proverbs 30:17).

As for if you should see fit to bind yourself, of the supererogations of the Laws, what is possible for you, after fulfilling and discharging your obligations — seeking the bounty after your intellect has agreed and your caprice has resisted — that is good. You are rewarded for it, and you have not gone outside the opinion of the early ones in it, for they said: "And make a fence for the Torah" (m. Avot 1:1), and they said: "Why was Jerusalem destroyed? Because they judged in it the strict letter of the Torah." When they were challenged on this saying, they said: "Because they made their words stand on the strict letter of the Torah and did not act inside the line of strict justice" (b. Bava Metzia 30b). And they said: "Rav Huna said: Whoever occupies himself with Torah alone is like one who has no God, as it is said: 'And many days for Israel without a true God' (2 Chronicles 15:3) — you have learned that there is no true God except in Torah and acts of loving-kindness." One of the excellent ones said: "Whoever has no supererogation has no obligation; supererogation is not accepted until the obligation has been discharged."

So they have permitted us — rather, have made obligatory upon us — the supererogation of adding to the obligations: like their saying "we add from the unconsecrated to the consecrated"; and supererogation by fasting in the daytime, by prayer, by charity, and by abandoning excess in the surpluses of permitted subsistence; and they have prohibited oath-taking by the name of God (mighty and exalted) even when the oath-taker is truthful; and the multitude of words even if it is safe from lying; and the report of the news of people even if it is safe from slander; and excess in praise even if its object is worthy; and excess in censure and hatred against the people of falling-short even if they deserve it. And much that resembles this.

It is fitting that we explicate of this second division examples by which the rest of the matters may be analogized, and that the human be on guard against them by God's help when he knows them comprehensively. There is no kind among the kinds of good but it has a misfortune that corrupts it; whoever stands upon the aspects of the misfortunes that corrupt the works has been more able to guard against them; whoever knows nothing but good alone, nothing of it is purified for him on account of the multitude of misfortunes that attach to it. One of the excellent ones used to say to his disciples: "Learn evil first, that you may avoid it; and learn good and act by it" — like the saying of Scripture: "Plow for yourselves a fallow field, and do not sow among thorns" (Jeremiah 4:3). Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai said, regarding the inner pockets that the deceivers of measures and weights insert: "Woe to me if I say, woe to me if I do not say. If I say, perhaps the deceivers will learn; if I do not say, perhaps the deceivers will say, the disciples of the wise are not skilled in our handiwork." Then they asked: did he say it, or not? They answered concerning this: "He said it; and from what verse? — *For the ways of the Lord are upright; the righteous walk in them, and the rebellious stumble in them*" (Hosea 14:10; b. Bava Metzia 60b).

I say that everything we have mentioned in this gate of what caprice tries to throw into doubt for the human — when he is unable to throw him into doubt about it, he takes to disputing him on it by argument and demonstration, that he may invalidate his realities for him. If you stand upon his deception and the weakness of his evidences, and he cannot withstand you nor overturn what you have known of certainty and validity from what has come before us in this gate — he turns to deceiving you and to confusing you about yourself. He says to you: "I am pleased by your state in the goodness of your conviction and your purification toward God (exalted be He). You have arrived at the ranks of bounty with God where no other than you in this present age has arrived; that is more than enough for you of thanks to God for His blessing upon you and His beneficence toward you. It would be fitting for you also to run to the discharging of some of the obligations of people, for you have known that they are causes of your benefit and your harm; that in their satisfaction with you is your glory and in their displeasure your deficiency. Use stratagem in what agrees with them and gives you favor with them — as our early ones said: 'Whoever the spirit of the creatures finds pleasing, the spirit of the Place finds pleasing' (m. Avot 3:10)."

You answer him: "What benefit is the dissembling toward a weak one like myself, who has in his power neither my benefit nor my harm? Scripture has said: 'Cease from man, in whose nostril is breath; for in what is he to be reckoned?' (Isaiah 2:22). Even if this were obligatory, how could I please all the people of my time when I do not have the power to please my own household, let alone others? As for what you have mentioned of the saying of the early ones in this concept — it is not such as to oblige stratagem in attracting the satisfaction of people; rather it is as one of the wise said in his testament to his son: 'My son, attracting the satisfaction of all created beings to yourself is not in your capacity; rather labor in the satisfaction of God toward you, and He will make created beings be satisfied with you,' as the Wise One said: 'When the Lord is pleased with the ways of a man, even his enemies he makes peaceful with him' (Proverbs 16:7). So too the one whom the multitude of the populace and the elect alike thank, praise his state, and are content with his actions — that is evidence that God (exalted be He) has planted love for him in the souls of people and has spread for him good fame upon their tongues; and that is among what God does not do for the one He hates. So this is a strong indicator of God's satisfaction with him. As for the excellent man's striving and exerting himself to obtain people's praise of him for his fine obedience to God, that is not from the way of the excellent ones."
Beware this and its likes from caprice's deceptions toward you. He aims by this only to lure you in, that he may cast you into the snares of ostentation.

So too you answer him in his praising of you: "And what is it you have admiringly-envied me for in my knowledge of the obligations of God (exalted be He) upon me? Is it anything but a charge against me before God, that I have not endured to act on what I know? And were I to act upon all that I know, would the totality of it suffice as thanks to God (mighty and exalted) for the slightest blessing among His blessings upon me? What measure has the span of my life in the span of the world? — and the whole of it would not suffice to describe God's blessings upon me; how then should I discharge what is incumbent upon me toward them, and what is binding for God upon me on their account?" Scripture said: "All flesh is grass, and all its kindness like the flower of the field" (Isaiah 40:6). One of our early ones used to say: "If I am not for myself, who is for me? And when I am for myself, what am I? And if not now — when?" (m. Avot 1:14).

When caprice despairs of his deceiving us by this aspect, he aims at it from the side of love of praise and acclaim in this world. He says to you: "I am pleased by your obedience to God, with the goodness of your reliance upon Him, your turning your affairs to Him, and the emptying of your heart from benefit by created beings to the exclusion of God; you are the truly purely-relying-on-God. It is not permissible for you to hide from people what you bear within of excellences. Rather it is incumbent upon you, since you have ruled your soul and reined in the reins of your appetite, to make manifest your work to people and reveal to them your school: there shall be for you in this honor in this world from them, and goodness of fame and name among them — as Scripture said: 'And I shall give them in My house and within My walls a hand and a name better than sons and daughters' (Isaiah 56:5); and He said: 'And I shall make for you a great name like the name of the great ones in the earth' (2 Samuel 7:9). Furthermore, they will pattern themselves upon your action; you will be rewarded through them. So conceal of your action only what you cannot spread and make manifest to people; you will gain the honor and praise in this world and abundant reward in the next."

You answer him: "What benefit is people's praise of me, the goodness of their saying about me, and their declaring me innocent — together with my knowledge of my falling-short in what is incumbent upon me of the right of God? And what does their honoring me and their righteousness toward me profit me, when they have no power for my benefit or for warding harm from me? Is their reckoning in this anything but the reckoning of the plant and the non-rational animal? Perhaps this will not be made complete for me from people if I aim at them in my work — falling into their imaginings as showy in my work — and so I deserve from them only hatred and censure; I would have corrupted my work by aiming at other than the face of God in it, and I would not have attained the praise from people in this world that I had hoped for."

It was said to one of the princes: "How is your finding-of-it-fine, the recitation of so-and-so?" — for he had a beautiful voice and beautiful melody when he recited the Book. He said: "How would the recitation of one whose recitation is for the sake of pleasing me and gaining favor with me please me? I would have found it fine for him only if he had aimed by it at the satisfaction of God (exalted be He) only."

So too the discourse on every one who aims, in his prayer, at people's finding it fine — among those of prayer in assemblies and the masters of the new spontaneous formulations: when their aim in them is people to the exclusion of God, they are not accepted with God.

You also say to him: "Perhaps, if honor accrues to me in this world for my work, nothing remains for me of its reward in the next, since I have hastened it in this world." It has been said of one of the righteous that he entered a market to buy a thing. He came down at one of the merchants, seeking to buy from him. The merchant's neighbor said to him: "Be lenient with him and meet his need, for he is of the people of scrupulousness and religion." The righteous man said to him: "I have no need of your leniency. I have come only to buy from you with my money, not with my religion." He refused to buy from him anything, and sought it from another who was ignorant of his affair.

As for what I mentioned of the saying "And I shall make for you a great name…" (2 Samuel 7:9) — its reckoning is the reckoning of the rest of the worldly hopes of people: of wealth and of honor that God bestows upon His saints when His wisdom requires that, as He said: "And also what you have not asked I have given you — both wealth and honor" (1 Kings 3:13); and He said: "Length of days is in her right hand; in her left, riches and honor" (Proverbs 3:16). The excellent ones, however, do not aim by their work at any of this; God (mighty and exalted) bestows it upon whomever He wills among the people of His obedience and other than them — among the believer and the unbeliever — as His wisdom requires, as He said: "And wealth and honor come from before You" (1 Chronicles 29:12).

You also answer him: "What is the measure of this world, even if my fame should fill it? What is the measure of the span of its breadth, even if my name should spread in it? How then, when my fame does not pass beyond the smallest part of its inhabited regions when it is great and renowned, and does not endure except for a brief span and is then forgotten as if it had never been? The Friend said: 'Surely the children of man are vapor; the children of men are a lie' (Psalms 62:10); and he said: 'His spirit goes out, he returns to his earth' (Psalms 146:4). The Wise One said: 'There is no remembrance of former things, nor of latter things that shall be — there shall be no remembrance of them' (Ecclesiastes 1:11). My preoccupation of soul with it and my aiming at it is a plain deficiency and a great error from me."

It has been related of one of the excellent ones that he said to a companion of his: "Are you equalized?" The companion said: "In what concept?" He said: "Praise and blame are equal in your eyes." He said: "No." He said to him: "If you have not yet attained, then exert yourself; perhaps you will reach this rank — for it is the highest rank of excellences and the limit of praiseworthy things."

When caprice despairs of deceiving you by this aspect, he aims at corrupting your work by preoccupying your mind with this world and its people and lengthening your hope and forgetting your term. When he sees that you wish to find leisure for the works of the next world — toward an obligatory or supererogatory prayer, or at the recitation of the Book of God, or at the learning of something of the science of religion and of *adab* — he whispers to you and preoccupies your inward with the news of your this-world: with the matters of commerce, of buying and selling, profit and loss. Then he says to you: "Take advantage of this seclusion and the leisure of this idleness, which you cannot achieve at other times on account of the constant pressure of preoccupations upon you. Reckon now with your partners, and verify what is for you and what is against you; what you have collected of your debts and what remains; what you should expose yourself to of the means of sustenance and what you should not; what has come before you of work and you congratulate yourself for it, or regret. If you have a dispute with another, summon it to your mind, and review all his arguments and yours, and what you can stratagem with at your dispute with him, that you may overcome him. So too if you have wealth or sheep or cattle or land that you sow, or service of a sultan or of subjects, or the accounting of the sultan or the subjects; or if you have debts upon you and you cannot pay them; or if you have brothers whose affairs require care of you and reckoning of yourself with them — let it run upon your mind in the time of the leisure of your soul for the work of obedience, whichever kind of these kinds it be — that he may preoccupy you with it and corrupt for you your work. For in the time of its work you are present with your body, absent with your heart and inner being."

If he does not preoccupy you with what we have mentioned, he sets running in your heart "he-said and it-was-said and protracted argument." If the human is among those who play with backgammon and chess and the like, he imagines that this is in front of him; he thinks about what he should do of advancing and delaying and the aspects of stratagem in the victory.

If he is safe from all that we have mentioned, and is of the people of knowledge and understanding, caprice runs in his mind some difficult concept among the concepts of knowledge, and preoccupies him with the question and the answer, the binding of the question and the loosing of it; what he has neglected of the matter of investigation and what remains upon him of the science. He reckons with himself for the work of it; and caprice imagines to him that this is among the totality of the work of obedience to God, and so corrupts for him the carrying-out of what would set him right. He may enter the work of obedience and exit from it, while wandering in the preoccupation of his soul with other than that of the matters of this world. He may seek God's forgiveness with his tongue while running with his thought and his inner being into disobedience to Him — of which one of the excellent ones said: "This forgiveness-asking of ours needs forgiveness-asking." He beseeches God with his limbs and is heedless of Him with his heart and his intent — like what Scripture said: "With his mouth and with his lips they have honored Me, but their heart is far from Me" (Isaiah 29:13); and He said: "And they enticed Him with their mouths and lied to Him with their tongues, while their heart was not steadfast with Him" (Psalms 78:36–37).

If, at this, you wake and reckon with your soul, and say to it: "How shall I treat the Creator (exalted be He) with what would not become me to treat created beings with — at my need of them and their need of me? For one whom I have approached for a need, and have asked the meeting of it with my tongue while being inattentive to him with my heart and inner being — were he to become aware of this from me, he would shun me and hate me, and would more rightly deny me my need. How then if he came to know that I am preoccupied of mind with what does not agree with his satisfaction, indeed with what angers him against me — his hatred for me would be more severe and his denying me more incumbent. By the like of this I would surely set against myself any who asked of me a need, when I was made aware of his secret state as God is made aware of the secret of my intent. How then am I not ashamed before my Creator that I should be content from myself toward Him with what I would not be content with from a weak one like me, and with which no created being needy and weak like me would be content from me? Scripture has said: 'Were they ashamed when they did abomination? They are not ashamed at all, neither do they know to blush' (Jeremiah 6:15)." — caprice is broken at this.

When caprice despairs of deceiving you from this aspect, he proposes that to you by way of *abandoning ostentation*. He says to you: "The completion of your purification toward God (exalted be He) is not made valid except by the negation of ostentation from you, much and little, fine and great. The negating of ostentation toward people from you is made valid only by the concealment of your work in its totality from them, and the manifesting of the contrary of what is in your inner being toward them. So when you pray, abridge; let no eagerness for it nor exertion in it appear from you. When you wish to learn something of knowledge, isolate yourself; let none other than God know it; let no excellence appear from you. Show forth heedlessness and slackness in the works of obedience, lest your name become famous through them and you forfeit your reward. Do not command the right or forbid the wrong, do not spread your knowledge, let no other benefit by it; let no mark of fear of God appear upon you, no sign among the signs of obedience to God, lest people honor you on account of that. The completion of the aspect of guarding-yourself is also that you befriend all the ranks of people and assume their dispositions; that you mingle with their company and run their course in seriousness and in jest; that you do not guard fully against lying and oaths; that you share with them in food, drink, conversation, surplus speech, and much laughter; that you take from them and recount their faults; and everything that negates from you the name of asceticism in this world and its people."

If you obey him in this, he strips you of your religion while you do not perceive it. But if you turn upon him and say to him: "You have advised me well, O my enemy, in your struggle against me and your subtlety with me — to demolish my strength and hasten my fall! How shall I flee from the fire to the burning sand? I am fleeing the love of praise and honor only that I should not strive in self-adornment toward people; and you command me to self-adorn toward them while neglecting obedience to God! It is fitting for me to conceal my work when it is sound and valid without people's knowing of it; but as for when it is among the works that are not made valid except by people's knowing of them — like prayer with a congregation, commanding the right and forbidding the wrong, the spreading of knowledge, doing-the-beautiful, and the like — it is not from prudence to abandon it and neglect it on account of ostentation; rather it is incumbent upon me to do it for the face of God (exalted be He). If I am praised for it and honored on its account, it does not harm me in my reward, since I did not aim at this in my work."

It has been said: "When you have done a work and people have come to know it, and you wish to stand upon the purity of your intent in it, test that of yourself by two aspects. The first: that you know what it is you sought by the work — of what recompense — and from whom you hoped for that. If from God, then it is pure; if from another, it is not pure. The second aspect: that you know of yourself, were you to be in private — would you do that work in that state? If this is made valid for you from yourself, your work is pure for God; multiply it. If less than that, leave it until your inner being is made clear in it for God."

When caprice does not find a way to deceive you by this aspect, he uses on you what is more subtle than that — by way of reward and punishment in this world and the next. He says to you: "You are among the choice of God and His elect; the like of you deserves the reward of this world and the next. Exert yourself according to your capacity that perhaps you may attain it by your work and by the goodness of your obedience to God. Make the reward set before your eyes; labor with all your effort to reach it, for it is the limit of your felicity and the end of your delight, as he said: 'Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart' (Psalms 97:11)."

If you obey him and lean upon his words, he throws you into a kind of hidden associationism. For you have made your soul your object of worship, since you exert yourself only in what gives you pleasure and joy, and ward off pain and sorrow from yourself. Were it not for your hope of this, you would have ceased thanks to God for His successive blessings upon you, and would not have made obedience to Him on their account binding upon yourself — together with [the fact that] you do not see Him as deserving of obedience and worship for His majesty and the magnitude of His power and the traces of His wisdom. About this our early ones (peace be upon them) said: "Do not be like the slaves who serve the master on condition of receiving a gift; rather be like the slaves who serve the master on condition of not receiving a gift; and let the fear of Heaven be upon you" (m. Avot 1:3).

When caprice despairs of you by these aspects we have mentioned, he throws you into the sea of doubts about the meanings of *jabr* and *ʿadl*. When he sees in you heedlessness of the works of obedience and inclination toward acts of disobedience, he aims to verify *jabr* with you by strong proofs from the written and the rational, that excuses may be widened upon you — saying to you: "Were God to will that you obey Him, He would have compelled you to that and constrained you upon it; nothing has been but what the predeterminations have run with. Do you contend with the decree, or struggle against the destiny? You are nothing but an instrument used in what He has used you in; the kingpin of all matters is in the hand of God (mighty and exalted), as Scripture said: 'I am the Lord, who does all'" (Isaiah 44:24).

When he sees you doing some work of the matters of this world and its causes, he says to you: "Beware of laziness and slack! Do not rely on any other than yourself, for good and evil are in your capacity, and action and refraining are in your power. Exert yourself and labor with all your effort to attain what you long for of the world's pleasures; and guard yourself from the causes of the disliked with all your power, that you may be safe from them — as the Wise One said: 'Snares and traps are in the way of the perverse; whoever guards his soul shall be far from them' (Proverbs 22:5); and: 'A man's folly perverts his way, and his heart frets against the Lord' (Proverbs 19:3); and: 'This is from your hand to you' (Malachi 1:9), and the like."
So he flips the proofs upon you — once with *jabr* and predetermination, and a second time with *justice* and *choice* — according to what agrees with him of his deception toward you and your sloth.

If you wake and bring to mind the saying of the early ones in this concept — "Everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven" (b. Berakhot 33b) — you labor in the matters of religion the labor of one for whom it has been validly established that by his work he is rewarded and punished, as the Wise One said: "For according to a man's deeds He shall recompense him" (Proverbs 24:12); and you run in the matters of this world the running of one for whom it has been validly established that the reins of all his movements and the turn of his affairs are in the decree of God (exalted be He) — and so he relies in all of them upon Him, and casts himself in them upon Him, as he said: "Cast upon the Lord your burden, and He shall sustain you" (Psalms 55:23).

When caprice despairs of deceiving you by what we have mentioned of aspects, he takes you in another aspect and says to you: "As for what you have resolved upon of obedience to God and the purifying of it for His face — you will catch up with this in the time to come. Even if there remained of your life one day, and you carried out His obedience, the way one ought, one day before your death, you would deserve the abiding reward with Him and have been delivered from punishment — for you have already known the aspects of repentance, and that He receives it from you when it is made valid from you in its proper aspects."

Return to your sound analogical reasoning and dispute him on this, and say to him: "How shall I be patient until the day before my death, when I do not know the day of my death? I would be like a slave of a sultan who had been assured by him that he would not remove him from his presence as long as his lifetime — and so exerted himself in the seeking of worldly pleasures, eager to apply himself, after that, to the service of his master. Between his eager pursuit and his eagerness, the sultan suddenly demanded him for service, and he had no excuse; so he deserved that he be cast out from his service and from all his lands. He went out from him poor and grieving over what he had not stored up for himself in his time of service to his sultan when it was possible — and remained the rest of his days poor, troubled, gloomy, grieving, censured, until the day of his death."

When caprice despairs of you by the aspects we have mentioned, he aims at it from the side of conceit, self-glory, and slightness of humility. He says to you: "By the bounty of God (exalted be He), you have reached the most excellent and most elevated of what the righteous and the truthful have come down to, in the truthfulness of your inner being and the purification of action by obedience to God; you are alone in your present age and singular among the people of your time. It is fitting that you make manifest your excellence over them by hatred of them, by undermining them, by mention of their evils, by the spreading of the badness of their inner beings; that you reproach and rebuke them for that, that they may be deterred and return to God in repentance over what has gone before from them — running upon the patterns of the prophets and the fathers (peace be upon them), as he said: 'You, son of man, declare to the house of Israel concerning the house, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities' (Ezekiel 43:10)."

You answer him: "How shall I hate and reproach the one whose inner being and intent toward God I have no knowledge of, even if his outer is hated? And though the prophets reproached and reproved the people of their time, that was by the permission of the Creator (exalted be He) to them and His showing-them the secret of those people and the corruption of their inner being. As for me, it is not in the power of my knowledge or my acquaintance to know what is in the inner beings or the contents of the secret places. Perhaps the inner of the one who is hated by me is much better than his outer — and what is my knowledge of him? Perhaps the inner of him is more excellent than mine before God (mighty and exalted) — and even if his outer is bad, perhaps his ignorance of the right of God upon him has carried him to that, and he is more entitled to excuse than I am, since my knowledge exceeds his. God demands of the human only according to his knowledge. So I am more entitled to hatred than he, on account of the surplus of my falling-short in what is incumbent upon me of obedience to God — together with my knowledge of that — over his falling-short with his ignorance of it. He disobeys God out of ignorance and inattention; I disobey Him out of knowledge and intent. Perhaps his vice is outer and apparent and his excellence inner and concealed — and I am the contrary of that — so he is more entitled with God to mercy and forgiveness than I, and his good deed is the equivalent of many of my good deeds, since God alone is informed of it: He is not praised for it, nor honored on its account; whereas I am the contrary of that, on account of the renown of my outer beauty over his. So too in the matter of acts of disobedience: my disobedience is the equivalent of many of his acts of disobedience, since my disobedience is hidden and concealed and his disobedience is manifest and renowned. So in people's hatred of him for it there is *purification* for him; the reward of my work in this world is diminished by its renown, and there remains for him the reward of his work for the next world; the punishment of his disobedience in this world is diminished by people's hatred of him for it, and there remains upon me the punishment of my disobedience for the next. Furthermore, when I preoccupy my soul with searching out the faults of people and tallying up their vices, I am prevented from working out my own deficiency and standing upon my own faults, which are more emphatic upon me and more binding for me — like the sick patient whose own sickness preoccupies him from working out the sicknesses of people, and the treatment of his own self from the treatment of others." Caprice is broken at this and routed before you.

If his arrows do not pierce you in what I have mentioned, he watches you in the times of your fortune and your misfortune. When your affairs run according to your desire, he says to you: "This is the fruit of your prudence, the subtlety of your contrivance, and the piercing of your understanding; exert yourself in the matters of your this-world, labor for them, that this state may endure for you and you may rise to what is above it. Take advantage of this leisure and enjoy in this period — for it would be as though your name had been called and you had answered your Lord into the darkness of the grave, where there is no work and no movement, no pleasure and no pain." He uses as his evidence for this the saying of the Wise One: "Whatever your hand finds to do, with your might do it; for there is no work or reasoning or knowledge or wisdom in Sheol, where you are going" (Ecclesiastes 9:10).

If you are in the state of your misfortune, he summons to your mind the felicity of the unbelievers and the bliss of the dissolute, as he said: "The tents of robbers are at peace, and those who provoke God are secure" (Job 12:6). And he says to you: "Your state has only become corrupted because you have bound yourself to obedience to God and the upholding of His commandments; and you have not the capacity to uphold this for the magnitude of its toil and the distance of its goal. Were you to throw it off yourself and rest from it, you would be admiringly-envied in your state — as you see those who disobey are. Do you not see the saying of the Messenger (peace be upon him), on God's behalf: 'In those who are near Me I shall be sanctified' (Leviticus 10:3); and He said: 'Only you have I known of all the families of the earth, therefore I shall visit upon you all your iniquities' (Amos 3:2), and the like?"

When he sees of you a resolve upon the work of any of the works of obedience, he magnifies the matter for you and frightens you from it. If it is among the matters of fasting and hunger, he says to you: "Beware! It will weaken you and sicken you and cut you off from the matters of your this-world and your next-world." If it is among the matters of supererogatory prayer at night, he gives you the imagining that sleep is more important for you than nourishment, more guarding for your health, and stronger for your body than food and drink. If it is among the matters of the *zakāh* and charity, he gives you the imagination of the loss of your wealth and pictures poverty between your eyes and makes you sense the abasement of indigence and want. So too in every kind among the kinds of excellences and obligations, he aims to frighten you and make the matter great in your soul that you may be lazy.
When you are about to do an act of disobedience, he makes its pleasure beloved to you and makes you forget its outcome; he makes you eager to do it and to incline toward it.

When you are sharp to the like of this from him, respond to him that every pain that has passed over you in what has gone before of your life has left no trace in you; rather it has gone quickly and waned swiftly. The reward for it remains for you forever, never ending. For one who fasts and then breaks his fast at night, it is as though he had not fasted; he returns to his strength, and the reward of his fast remains preserved. So too the one who keeps watch part of the night — when he sleeps he returns to his alertness, as though he had not been awake; and the reward of his standing and the bounty of his prayer remain for him forever. As for the matter of the *zakāh*, I have explicated it in the Gate of Reliance with sufficient explanation. As for the matter of the acts of disobedience: repeat in your soul, summon to your mind the swift departure of their pleasure — what is permitted of them and what is forbidden — and the remaining of the disgrace of what is ugly among them upon you, and their punishment in this world and the next.
At this, caprice is routed before you, and you are alert to good work and lazy concerning every ugly work.

If he despairs of you in this aspect, and you have set your resolve and have done some of the obediences, he aims to introduce griefs into your heart and the succession of sorrows upon you, that regret may fall upon you for what has come before of good work — that he may deprive you of the reward upon it and of God's acceptance of it from you. If you have done something of the acts of disobedience, he aims to introduce joy into your heart and gladness in what has come before to you — that he may strengthen your judgment by that and make you eager toward it. If you are sharp to his stratagem and aware of his various snares, you are on guard from them; you take help from God in delivering yourself from them. If you are not aware of them, he throws you down suddenly and unloads his arrows upon you in heedlessness, as Scripture said: "Until an arrow split his liver, like the bird hastening to the snare, and he did not know that it was for his soul" (Proverbs 7:23).

If you stand against him in all this and he cannot deceive you by what we have mentioned, he aims at it from the side of your knowledge. If he sees in you eagerness for the learning of knowledge, he says to you: "Does there not satisfy you what satisfies the great of the people of your present age and your shaykhs of acquaintance with your Truthful Book? Do you not know that knowledge has no end and no limit? Aim at the eye of religion and the root of the Law; then learn what you can adorn yourself by before people — of the meaning of poetry and prosody, the science of rare lexicography, the unusual hadith, the popular proverb. And let go from yourself of the news of jurisprudence and the disputes of the scholars in it. Do not expose yourself to the science of the roots of demonstration, the elements of speech, the kinds of analogical reasoning, the modes of evidence, the manner in which the cause runs alongside the caused, and the agreement of manifest knowledge with hidden knowledge — on account of its obscurity and the subtlety of its meanings. Imitate the people of transmission in what you can stand upon its validity, as you imitate them in what is impossible for you to stand upon."

If you do not accept from him, and take up prudence for yourself, he shoots you with the arrow of envy toward your companions. If they have attained knowledge to the exclusion of you, you bear a grudge against them; you aim at their fault-finding, their undermining, the mention of their faults, as if they had stripped you of your understanding and seized your knowledge. If you have attained to the exclusion of them, you undermine them by the surplus of your understanding; despise them for their ignorance; make manifest that to the populace; and become conceited with yourself and proud of your understanding — to the point that you claim knowledge of what you do not know; you scorn learning; you tilt your nose at being taught; you are agitated when objected to; you multiply claims of knowledge; you adorn yourself by ignorance-attribution-to-your-companions; you adorn yourself by reproach of your peers — and so you are stripped of the manners of the people of knowledge of God and of His religion.

If what he aimed at of deceiving you from the side of knowledge does not come to him, he aims at it from the side of working at obedience. That is: when you do for God a work, he raises it in your eye, makes you conceited with it, and renders the people of your present age contemptible to you. He makes their hating, reproaching, and rebuking them easy for you — though perhaps they are with God more excellent than you. And if there is in your companions one of more excellent obedience to God, of more beautiful action toward Him, of greater exertion in nearing toward Him than you, caprice envies on your behalf and says to you: "O you, every excellence that has appeared from this one in obedience to God is a manifest deficiency of yours; were it not for him, you would be with people, then with God, the most excellent in your present age. Begrudge him; envy him; resent him; investigate his faults and his contradictions; watch his slips; observe his heedlessnesses; spread of that what you can; censure him with it; and if it is permissible for you to fabricate against him with falsehood that his name may fall with people — do it."

You answer him: "How shall I hate one whom God loves; and despise one whom God has bestowed bounty upon? Has my own incapacity for upholding the obedience of my Lord like his upholding it not been enough for me — that I should resent the one who has obeyed Him? This is not justice for the right of God (exalted be He). Rather it is incumbent upon me to love the one whom God loves, with love for His sake, and to honor the one whom God honors, in honor for the sake of God — as He said: 'And to those who fear the Lord, He gives honor' (Psalms 15:4). You have known what came in the story of Miriam in the matter of 'And Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses' (Numbers 12:1), and what came in the story of Korah and his followers in their envy of Aaron in their drawing-near to the light of God."

Now that we have explicated for you in this gate the totality of the roots of the corrupters of purification of action for God (exalted be He), and clarified the medicines for them according to our perception — it remains for us to call attention to one matter that is the kingpin of the whole.

The kingpin is *watchful awareness of God by the heart at the time of every act*. The body has its watchful awareness from the limbs whose movements people can see; the heart has its watchful awareness from God who searches the inward. To stand, at every act, in the consciousness that *God is watching*, and to perform the act with that consciousness as the operative interior — that is what makes the act, in its inwardness, a duty-of-the-heart performance and not merely a duty-of-the-limbs performance. The two duties may take place in a single act of, say, prayer; what distinguishes the prayer that is heart-and-limbs from the prayer that is limbs-only is the active *murāqaba* of God under whose gaze the prayer is taking place.

This concept will be developed in its proper gate (*Bāb al-murāqaba*, the Eighth Gate). What is required here is only the recognition that, without this watchful awareness, the work of *ikhlāṣ* in this gate cannot be completed — for the rest of the disciplines we have laid out are stratagems by the believer against his own caprice, and stratagems can be tricked. *Murāqaba*, by contrast, cannot be tricked: if one is genuinely standing under God's gaze, the question of *ikhlāṣ* is not a question one has to ask oneself, since the answer is settled by the gaze itself.

For this reason, the early ones said: "Know what is above you — a seeing eye, and a hearing ear, and all your deeds in a book are written" (m. Avot 2:1). The triple formula — *seeing eye, hearing ear, all deeds in a book* — is the rabbinic articulation of *murāqaba* applied to a Jewish-pious life: the believer who carries with him, at every moment, the consciousness that God sees, hears, and records, has built into his ordinary day the watchful awareness that this gate has been recommending. The Sufi teaching of *murāqaba* is not, in this respect, foreign to the rabbinic tradition; it is the same teaching, articulated in different vocabulary.

I have set out for you in this gate the totality of the roots of the corrupters of purification of action for God, and have called attention to its medicines according to my perception. Whoever desires to add to it from the rest of the matters of caprice and the explication of its stratagems will find what is sufficient for him, with God's aid (exalted be He). My intent in what I have laid down has been only the indication of the way and the gesture toward the path, that whoever desires guidance may be guided. As Scripture said: "Whoever is wise will hear these things and will consider the kindnesses of the Lord" (Psalms 107:43).

In what I have mentioned in this gate is sufficiency for whoever seeks guidance and asks for the truth for its own sake, and seeks knowledge for its essence. May God grant us and you success in what is His obedience, by His mercy.

The Fifth Gate is complete, on the explication of the aspects of the obligation of the purification of action for the face of God and the safeguarding from ostentation. With its completion, the First Part of the Book of the Guide to the Duties of the Heart is complete, by the help of God and His grace (exalted be He).
